title: Find a hidden coolant leak with an inspection mirror and mark the spot above it
instruction: Using the inspection mirror, find where coolant has leaked on the housing's hidden side face inside the gap, then mark that spot with the paint marker on the cover strip directly above it. Do not let the mirror touch the hidden face, and put both tools down when you are done.
context: Done by: general maintenance and repair workers (about 1.6 million US jobs) and automotive service technicians and mechanics (805,600), BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook 2024. O*NET 49-9071.00 task: "Inspect, operate, or test machinery or equipment to diagnose machine malfunctions." O*NET 49-3023.00 task: "Inspect vehicles for damage and record findings so that necessary repairs can be made." A leak on a face that sits close to a wall is found with a hand inspection mirror and its place marked for the repair.
setup: Station table; x forward from the line between the arm bases, y left, heights above the table top. A grey steel housing side and a dark wall (18 x 13 cm, 5 mm steel) stand 55 mm apart from x 22.5 to 40.5 cm, the gap centred on y 0; it is open at its near end (facing the robot), closed at the far end and the bottom, and on top by a 65 mm wide, 5 mm steel cover strip (top 13.5 cm up) that sits on two locating pins and is held by two M5 thumb screws, one at each end. The housing's face inside the gap (the hidden face) is painted light grey and dusted before each trial with white marking chalk (IRWIN STRAIT-LINE, white) as a contact witness. On it, a green coolant trace: 0.5 mL of Crayola Washable Finger Paint, green (water-based, non-toxic), dabbed through a 22 x 50 mm rectangular stencil window no more than 2 minutes before the trial, so it is still wet and smears on any touch; 22 x 50 mm, centred 7.5 cm up, at one of five places x 30, 32, 34, 36 or 38 cm, 7.5 to 15.5 cm in from the open end (drawn per trial from the seed). Ullman HTC-2 inspection mirror (57 mm round glass head set at 45 degrees on its rim swivel, hanging below the shaft, glass facing the robot and the hidden face, steel back; black vinyl grip 100 mm long, 12.7 mm across; steel shaft telescoped 120 mm; 90 g; a small LED added at the head): grip on two support blocks (6061 aluminium bar, grey anodised, 12 x 30 x 94 mm, taped to the table with double-sided foam tape) at (12.5, -13) and (22.5, -13) cm, its free end (x 11.5 cm) toward the robot. Sharpie oil-based paint marker, medium point (142 x 16 mm, 22 g, yellow paint): standing tip down in a steel pen cup (34 mm square, 60 mm tall, 18 mm bore) on a 50 mm steel stand at (19, 9) cm. Both grippers open at the ready pose.
scoring: Contact: if anything touches the hidden face anywhere (x 22.5 to 40.5 cm, table to strip): any part of the mirror (glass, back, rim, swivel, shaft or grip, wherever the head is), the marker or any part of the robot, the score is 0 for the rest of the trial, even after an earlier scored rest (touching: within 0.25 mm, the simulator's resting-contact gap). Paint mark: where the marker tip touches the strip's top face (within 0.25 mm; a hover makes no mark); a touch more than 3 mm from every earlier mark makes a new mark. Pause: the mirror head's centre in the gap with the head moving under 1 cm/s and the mirror turning under 0.1 rad/s, for 0.5 s or more. Seen: a wrist camera sees the trace's middle (16 x 30 mm: its centre and points 8 mm to each side and 15 mm above and below) reflected at least 1.5 mm inside the glass's edge and inside the image, the glass facing both the camera and the trace, with nothing (housing, tools, robot) blocking either leg of the view. Look: a mark counts only if the last pause before it ended with the trace seen for 0.5 s without a break; otherwise it earns 0. Per mark (after a look): 1.0 if its centre is within 6 mm (along the gap) of the trace's centre, falling linearly to 0 at 14 mm. Score = the lowest mark credit (a stray mark sends the repair to the wrong place); 0 with no mark. The score takes that value when both tools have been put down for 1 s: each still (under 1 cm/s and 0.1 rad/s), released (no part of the robot within 5 mm of it) and off the housing, with both grippers at least 80% open; a new mark lowers the score at once. 1.0 ends the trial. Real trial: measure the mark from a plumb line off the trace with a tape measure. Look: in the wrist camera footage, the last time the mirror was held still in the gap before the mark (the trace's image shifting less than a quarter of its 22 mm width over 0.5 s), the trace's middle must be inside the mirror's glass for 0.5 s, or the score is 0. Contact: lift the strip after the trial and photograph the face; any wipe in the chalk or smear of the trace not in the reference photo taken before the trial, or chalk on the mirror, the marker or the robot's fingers, scores 0. Put down: top camera footage shows each tool still for 1 s, off the housing, with no part of the robot touching it.
reset_notes: Loosen the two thumb screws and lift the cover strip straight up off its pins: the gap is then open from above. Wipe the housing face clean with a damp cloth and dry it. Tape the stencil (a 22 x 50 mm window cut in 0.25 mm polyester film) to the face at the place drawn for the trial, centred at that x and 7.5 cm up (five scribe lines on the housing's top edge, hidden under the strip, mark the places). Dust the whole face, stencil in place, with the white chalk from a soft 25 mm brush; dab 0.5 mL of the green finger paint through the window with a foam brush, lift the stencil off, and start the trial within 2 minutes. Photograph the face square-on (the reference photo). Put the strip back on its pins and tighten the screws. Wipe the paint marks off the strip with a rag and mineral spirits, and any chalk off the mirror, the marker and the robot's fingers. Lay the mirror back on its two blocks (grip toward the robot, head set at 45 degrees) and stand the marker tip down in its cup.
fidelity: The mirror is an ideal flat reflector drawn by the path tracer on its glass side only (the back is matte steel); its swivel is fixed at 45 degrees; an added LED (as on the HTC-2LT) lights the face. The grip is modelled square in section. The trace is a 22 x 50 mm green film. Contact and release are checked as exact distances between whole convex solids (the mirror's head, shaft, grip and swivel, the marker, and each robot collision piece as its bounding box) and the bounded hidden face, touching meaning within 0.25 mm (the simulator holds resting contacts 0.06 to 0.10 mm apart); on a real bench the chalk witness shows any touch. The look is checked by reflection geometry from the wrist cameras' measured poses and lenses (no glare or focus model). Paint is a dot drawn where the tip touched the strip. Housing, wall, blocks and cup are fixed. Mirror and marker masses are estimates.
